summary: Still Answering is a 30-second animated film, with an interactive landing page, for kids aged 8 to 14 about the machines NASA left behind on the Moon, on Mars and in deep space. Instead of listing facts, the film follows one beam of light out from Earth. A clock on screen counts how long that light takes to reach three machines, using real distances for this week from NASA JPL Horizons. It takes 1.3 seconds to reach the Apollo 11 laser mirror, which scientists still bounce lasers off. It takes about 11 minutes to reach Ingenuity, the Mars helicopter built to fly up to 5 times that flew 72. And it takes a whole day to reach Voyager 1, which on 18 November 2026 becomes the first human-made object one light-day from Earth. On the landing page, kids can fire a laser at the Moon and use a light clock for any day in November. It turns "abandoned" hardware into something kids can feel: a blink to the Moon, minutes to Mars, a day to Voyager. It also shows that some of these machines are still answering.
details:
What it does

Still Answering introduces school-age space fans to hardware NASA left behind, and to the science it made possible and still makes possible. It has two parts:

- A 30-second animated film (1080p, English narration, English captions burned in).

- An interactive landing page that tells the story as you scroll.

It answers the challenge with a story rather than a list of facts.

How it works

The whole film is one journey of light. A green laser pulse leaves Earth and the camera follows it.

- The Moon: the pulse reaches Tranquility Base, where Apollo 11 left a laser retroreflector in 1969 (a panel of 100 corner-cube mirrors). It bounces straight back. Scientists on Earth still time these bounces, and that is how we know the Moon is slowly drifting away.

- Mars: the camera races on to Ingenuity at its final airfield, shown accurately with all four blades broken. It was built to fly up to 5 times and flew 72.

- Deep space: radio waves race back from Voyager 1. On 18 November 2026 it will be so far away that light takes a whole day to reach it. No human-made object has been that far before.

- The camera pulls back to a map of where everything is this week. The film ends on a simple recap of all three machines.

A clock in the corner shows how long light from Earth takes to reach each machine: 1.32 seconds, then 10 minutes 56 seconds, then 24 hours. It's the hero number of the film, and it comes straight from NASA data.

The landing page goes further. As you scroll, each machine is revealed in turn. A "Fire the laser!" button times light's real 2.6-second round trip to the Apollo 11 mirror. A light-clock playground lets you pick the Moon, Ingenuity or Voyager 1 and any day in November 2026, and shows the distance, the light time and how many trips around Earth that is, all from daily NASA JPL Horizons data. It ends with "Hope you learnt something new!"

NASA data at the core

Every distance and light time comes from NASA JPL Horizons. Our calculation of Voyager 1's one-light-day moment matches NASA's published time (18 Nov 2026, 10:16:07 UTC) to the second. The scenes are real-time 3D renders of NASA's own 3D models (Apollo Lunar Module, Ingenuity, Voyager) on NASA maps of Earth, the Moon and Mars. The sound includes real NASA recordings: Voyager 1's plasma waves and Mars wind recorded by Perseverance.

Benefits and impact

Kids usually hear only about missions that are still active. Still Answering gives forgotten machines a story and connects each piece of hardware to the science it did and still does. The light clock makes huge distances understandable in seconds. We hope kids leave curious about what else is out there, and remember that there's a mirror on the Moon that scientists still use.

How it is creative

Instead of a gallery of old spacecraft, the project uses one idea, the time it takes light to travel, as a single thread from the Moon to the edge of the solar system. The machines are shown where and as they really are this week. The hero number comes straight from NASA data rather than being added on top.

Factors we considered

- Accuracy: every claim was traced to a NASA page and checked by a separate fact-checking pass. Fixes included all four of Ingenuity's blades being broken (not one), NASA's exact "up to five flights", radio (not laser) for Voyager, and real positions on the map.

- Age group: plain language, big bold text in Atkinson Hyperlegible (a typeface designed for easy reading), captions that highlight each word as it's spoken, and a green dot for "still working".

- Accessibility: captions on every narrated line, high contrast, and a page that works on phones.

- Rules: the demo is 29.5 seconds. AI use is labelled on screen and in the file metadata. No NASA logos or flags appear. No people appear in the film.

Tools

Remotion, React, three.js and React Three Fiber (3D animation and rendering); TypeScript, HTML/CSS/JavaScript and Python; NASA JPL Horizons API; Kokoro text-to-speech (AI voice); faster-whisper (caption timing); NumPy, SciPy and pyloudnorm (original music and sound, mixed to -14 LUFS); FFmpeg.
